q-16172.name: Question 1
q-16172.problem:
The functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are differentiable on an open interval containing $x=7.$ The values of $f,$ $g,$ and their respective derivatives are shown in the following table:

| $x$ | $f(x)$ | ${f}^{′}(x)$ | $g(x)$ | ${g}^{′}(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $7$ | $0$ | $1$ | $0$ | $2$ |

$$

$$

Find ${lim}_{x\to 7}\frac{f(x)}{{x}^{2}g(x)}.$
q-16172.worked_solution:
Notice that if we try to substitute $x=7$ directly into the limit, we reach the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 7}\frac{f(x)}{{x}^{2}g(x)} & ={\frac{f(x)}{{x}^{2}g(x)}|}_{x=7} \\  & =\frac{f(7)}{{7}^{2}\cdot g(7)} \\  & =\frac{0}{49\cdot 0} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we use L'Hopital's rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 7}\frac{f(x)}{{x}^{2}g(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to 7}\frac{(f(x))^{′}}{({x}^{2}g(x))^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 7}\frac{{f}^{′}(x)}{2xg(x)+{x}^{2}{g}^{′}(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=7$ again, and this time, we are actually able to determine the result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 7}\frac{{f}^{′}(x)}{2xg(x)+{x}^{2}{g}^{′}(x)} & ={\frac{{f}^{′}(x)}{2xg(x)+{x}^{2}{g}^{′}(x)}|}_{x=7} \\  & =\frac{{f}^{′}(7)}{2\cdot 7\cdot g(7)+{7}^{2}\cdot {g}^{′}(7)} \\  & =\frac{1}{0+49\cdot 2} \\  & =\frac{1}{98}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${lim}_{x\to 7}\frac{f(x)}{{x}^{2}g(x)}=\frac{1}{98}.$

The functions f(x) and g(x) are differentiable on an open interval containing x=7. The values of f, g, and their respective derivatives are shown in the following table:

x f(x) f′(x) g(x) g′(x)
7 0 1 0 2
Find limx→7f(x)x2g(x).

a
17
b
−7
c
198

49

Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that if we try to substitute x=7 directly into the limit, we reach the indeterminate form 00.

limx→7f(x)x2g(x)=f(x)x2g(x)|x=7=f(7)72⋅g(7)=049⋅0=00

So, we use L'Hopital's rule:

limx→7f(x)x2g(x)=limx→7(f(x))′(x2g(x))′=limx→7f′(x)2xg(x)+x2g′(x)

We substitute x=7 again, and this time, we are actually able to determine the result: limx→7f′(x)2xg(x)+x2g′(x)=f′(x)2xg(x)+x2g′(x)|x=7=f′(7)2⋅7⋅g(7)+72⋅g′(7)=10+49⋅2=198

Therefore, limx→7f(x)x2g(x)=198.

q-16174.name: Question 2
q-16174.problem:
The functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are twice-differentiable on an open interval containing $x=10.$ The values of $f,$ $g,$ and their respective derivatives are given below:

| $x$ | $f(x)$ | ${f}^{′}(x)$ | ${f}^{″}(x)$ | $g(x)$ | ${g}^{′}(x)$ | ${g}^{″}(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $10$ | $-5$ | $0$ | $3$ | $-20$ | $-2$ | $-6$ |

$$

$$

Find ${lim}_{x\to 10}\frac{f(x)+5}{2x+g(x)}.$
q-16174.worked_solution:
Notice that if we try to substitute $x=10$ directly into the limit, we reach the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 10}\frac{f(x)+5}{2x+g(x)} & ={\frac{f(x)+5}{2x+g(x)}|}_{x=10} \\  & =\frac{f(10)+5}{20+g(10)} \\  & =\frac{-5+5}{20+(-20)} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we use L'Hopital's rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 10}\frac{f(x)+5}{2x+g(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to 10}\frac{(f(x)+5)^{′}}{(2x+g(x))^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 10}\frac{{f}^{′}(x)}{2+{g}^{′}(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=10$ again, but once more, we reach the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 10}\frac{{f}^{′}(x)}{2+{g}^{′}(x)} & ={\frac{{f}^{′}(x)}{2+{g}^{′}(x)}|}_{x=10} \\  & =\frac{{f}^{′}(10)}{2+{g}^{′}(10)} \\  & =\frac{0}{2+(-2)} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

We apply L'Hopital's rule again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 10}\frac{{f}^{′}(x)}{2+{g}^{′}(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to 10}\frac{({f}^{′}(x))^{′}}{(2+{g}^{′}(x))^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 10}\frac{{f}^{″}(x)}{{g}^{″}(x)},\end{aligned}
$$

and this time, when we substitute $x=10,$ we are actually able to determine the result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 10}\frac{{f}^{″}(x)}{{g}^{″}(x)} & ={\frac{{f}^{″}(x)}{{g}^{″}(x)}|}_{x=10} \\  & =\frac{{f}^{″}(10)}{{g}^{″}(10)} \\  & =\frac{3}{-6} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${lim}_{x\to 10}\frac{f(x)+5}{2x+g(x)}=-\frac{1}{2}.$

Therefore, limx→10f(x)+52x+g(x)=−12.

q-337001.name: Question 3
q-337001.problem:
The functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are differentiable on an open interval containing $x=2.$ The values of $f,$ $g,$ and their respective derivatives are shown in the following table:

| $x$ | $f(x)$ | ${f}^{′}(x)$ | $g(x)$ | ${g}^{′}(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $2$ | $1$ | $3$ | $3$ | $4$ |

Using the values from the table, evaluate the following limit:

${lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{\sqrt{x+g(x)}-\sqrt{5}}{f(x)+x-3}=$
{{field-1}}
q-337001.worked_solution:
Notice that if we try to substitute $x=2$ directly into the limit, we reach the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{\sqrt{x+g(x)}-\sqrt{5}}{f(x)+x-3} & ={\frac{\sqrt{x+g(x)}-\sqrt{5}}{f(x)+x-3}|}_{x=2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2+g(2)}-\sqrt{5}}{f(2)+2-3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2+3}-\sqrt{5}}{1+2-3} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we use L'Hopital's rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{\sqrt{x+g(x)}-\sqrt{5}}{f(x)+x-3} & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{(\sqrt{x+g(x)}-\sqrt{5})^{′}}{(f(x)+x-3)^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{\frac{1+{g}^{′}(x)}{2\sqrt{x+g(x)}}}{{f}^{′}(x)+1}\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=2$ again, and this time, we are actually able to determine the result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{\frac{1+{g}^{′}(x)}{2\sqrt{x+g(x)}}}{{f}^{′}(x)+1} & ={\frac{\frac{1+{g}^{′}(x)}{2\sqrt{x+g(x)}}}{{f}^{′}(x)+1}|}_{x=2} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1+{g}^{′}(2)}{2\sqrt{2+g(2)}}}{{f}^{′}(2)+1} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1+4}{2\sqrt{5}}}{3+1} \\  & =\frac{5}{8\sqrt{5}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{\sqrt{x+g(x)}-\sqrt{5}}{f(x)+x-3}=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{8}.
$$

q-337014.name: Question 4
q-337014.problem:
The functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are twice-differentiable on an open interval containing $x=1.$ The values of $f,$ $g,$ and their respective derivatives are given below:

| $x$ | $f(x)$ | ${f}^{′}(x)$ | ${f}^{″}(x)$ | $g(x)$ | ${g}^{′}(x)$ | ${g}^{″}(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $e$ | $0$ | $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $2$ |

Using the values from the table, evaluate the following limit:

${lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{e}^{x}-x\,f(x)}{\,f(x)g(x)-{e}^{x}\,}=$
{{field-1}}
q-337014.worked_solution:
Notice that if we try to substitute $x=1$ directly into the limit, we reach the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{e}^{x}-xf(x)}{f(x)g(x)-{e}^{x}} & ={\frac{{e}^{x}-xf(x)}{f(x)g(x)-{e}^{x}}|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{1}-1\cdot f(1)}{f(1)g(1)-{e}^{1}} \\  & =\frac{e-e}{(e)(1)-e} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we use L'Hopital's rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{e}^{x}-xf(x)}{f(x)g(x)-{e}^{x}} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{({e}^{x}-xf(x))^{′}}{(f(x)g(x)-{e}^{x})^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{e}^{x}-(f(x)+x{f}^{′}(x))}{{f}^{′}(x)g(x)+f(x){g}^{′}(x)-{e}^{x}}\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=1$ again, and once more we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{{e}^{x}-(f(x)+x{f}^{′}(x))}{{f}^{′}(x)g(x)+f(x){g}^{′}(x)-{e}^{x}}|}_{x=1} & =\frac{{e}^{1}-(f(1)+1\cdot {f}^{′}(1))}{{f}^{′}(1)g(1)+f(1){g}^{′}(1)-{e}^{1}} \\  & =\frac{e-(e+0)}{(0)(1)+(e)(1)-e} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{e}^{x}-(f(x)+x{f}^{′}(x))}{{f}^{′}(x)g(x)+f(x){g}^{′}(x)-{e}^{x}} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{({e}^{x}-(f(x)+x{f}^{′}(x)))^{′}}{({f}^{′}(x)g(x)+f(x){g}^{′}(x)-{e}^{x})^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{e}^{x}-(2{f}^{′}(x)+x{f}^{″}(x))}{{f}^{″}(x)g(x)+2{f}^{′}(x){g}^{′}(x)+f(x){g}^{″}(x)-{e}^{x}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now we substitute $x=1$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{{e}^{x}-(2{f}^{′}(x)+x{f}^{″}(x))}{{f}^{″}(x)g(x)+2{f}^{′}(x){g}^{′}(x)+f(x){g}^{″}(x)-{e}^{x}}|}_{x=1} & =\frac{{e}^{1}-(2{f}^{′}(1)+1\cdot {f}^{″}(1))}{{f}^{″}(1)g(1)+2{f}^{′}(1){g}^{′}(1)+f(1){g}^{″}(1)-{e}^{1}} \\  & =\frac{e-(2(0)+0)}{(0)(1)+2(0)(1)+(e)(2)-e} \\  & =\frac{e}{e} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{e}^{x}-x\,f(x)}{\,f(x)g(x)-{e}^{x}\,}=1.
$$

q-337304.problem:
The functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are twice-differentiable on an open interval containing $x=1.$ The values of $f,$ $g,$ and their respective derivatives are given below:

| $x$ | $f(x)$ | ${f}^{′}(x)$ | ${f}^{″}(x)$ | $g(x)$ | ${g}^{′}(x)$ | ${g}^{″}(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ | $-2$ | $4$ | $3$ | $-2$ | $2$ |

Using the values from the table, evaluate the following limit:

${lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\,f(x)+{x}^{2}-3\,}{\,g(x)+{x}^{2}-4\,}=$
{{field-1}}
q-337304.worked_solution:
Notice that if we try to substitute $x=1$ directly into the limit, we reach the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{f(x)+{x}^{2}-3}{g(x)+{x}^{2}-4} & ={\frac{f(x)+{x}^{2}-3}{g(x)+{x}^{2}-4}|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{f(1)+{1}^{2}-3}{g(1)+{1}^{2}-4} \\  & =\frac{2+1-3}{3+1-4} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we use L'Hopital's rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{f(x)+{x}^{2}-3}{g(x)+{x}^{2}-4} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(f(x)+{x}^{2}-3)^{′}}{(g(x)+{x}^{2}-4)^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{′}(x)+2x}{{g}^{′}(x)+2x}\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=1$ again, and once more we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{{f}^{′}(x)+2x}{{g}^{′}(x)+2x}|}_{x=1} & =\frac{{f}^{′}(1)+2(1)}{{g}^{′}(1)+2(1)} \\  & =\frac{-2+2}{-2+2} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{′}(x)+2x}{{g}^{′}(x)+2x} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{({f}^{′}(x)+2x)^{′}}{({g}^{′}(x)+2x)^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{″}(x)+2}{{g}^{″}(x)+2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now we substitute $x=1$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{{f}^{″}(x)+2}{{g}^{″}(x)+2}|}_{x=1} & =\frac{{f}^{″}(1)+2}{{g}^{″}(1)+2} \\  & =\frac{4+2}{2+2} \\  & =\frac{6}{4} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\,f(x)+{x}^{2}-3\,}{\,g(x)+{x}^{2}-4\,}=\frac{3}{2}.
$$
